title: Let's Zoom It Out
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Writing from inside "DEVOLSON" -- the Dark Evil Vortex of Late September-October-November, a term he borrows from teacher-blogger Kelly Treleaven -- Stuart describes the emotional whiplash of the fall teaching season, where confidence and exhaustion can trade places within a single week. After a day where his planned writing simply wouldn't come, he printed out a "Life in Weeks" grid and doodled on it, confronting how few weeks he has left in an average lifespan, in his kids' childhoods, and in a typical 30-year teaching career. Rather than finding the exercise morbid, he uses it to shift into appreciation, noticing that the zoomed-out view left him more grateful, tranquil, and fulfilled than the day before, even though the day itself was just as tiring. The piece functions as both a permission slip for teachers mid-slump and a concrete practice -- the weeks-grid zoom-out -- for converting DEVOLSON's disorientation into gratitude.
points: Stuart names a widely felt but rarely articulated seasonal experience -- DEVOLSON -- validating that cycling between "I've got it" and "I've lost it" within days is a normal, near-universal part of the fall teaching stretch.
His concrete practice is the "Life in Weeks" grid: printing out and doodling on a visual representation of a human lifespan in weeks to make the scarcity of time tangible rather than abstract.

Rather than landing in despair, the exercise redirects him toward appreciation -- he explicitly reports feeling more gratitude, tranquility, and fulfillment on the day he did the zoom-out than the day before.

The essay models emotional honesty as a move for teachers: admitting a day of planned writing simply didn't happen, and choosing rest (a nap, a walk) over forcing productivity, before returning to the work.
quotes: One day, I feel like I've got it; the next day, like I've lost it; the next, wondering what "it" even is. It's amazing that this job does this to me even after almost two decades.
If teaching is anything, it's a full buffet of the human experience.

I've got less than half of the number of weeks left in my life that an average US male gets. I've already lived through more than half of the number of weeks I'll have with my children still being children.
Some might find it a morbid exercise — and it could be, I guess. But I don't let it land me there. Instead, where I have it land me is in appreciation.

Today was another tiring day of teaching. It had a lot of those emotions on the pillow, just like yesterday did. But I definitely felt more gratitude, more tranquility, more fulfillment, more acceptance than I did yesterday.
It's kind of funny to me that DEVOLSON still catches me off guard. Like most teachers, in August I have an optimistic sense of what I want to work on during the school year.
